subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, Whipple
vignette: A 34-year-old man reports crampy abdominal pain and watery diarrhea within an hour of drinking milk. Symptoms improve when he avoids dairy. Stool pH is low, and a lactose hydrogen breath test shows a rise of 28 ppm above baseline after lactose ingestion. Endoscopy shows normal-appearing villi.
question: Which mechanism best explains this patient's diarrhea?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of enterocytes with villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis
Bacterial overgrowth deconjugating bile salts and impairing micelle formation
Inadequate pancreatic enzyme secretion causing maldigestion of fat and protein
Lactase deficiency with unabsorbed lactose drawing water into the lumen and colonic fermentation
Excessive bile acid delivery to the colon from altered enterohepatic circulation

explanation_correct: Lactose intolerance results from lactase deficiency at the brush border. Unhydrolyzed lactose remains in the intestinal lumen and exerts an osmotic effect, producing watery diarrhea; colonic bacteria ferment lactose to short-chain acids, lowering stool pH and increasing breath hydrogen (>20 ppm above baseline is positive). Villi are normally appearing unless lactase deficiency is secondary to injury at the villus tips, as after viral enteritis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes is celiac disease, which would show abnormal D-xylose absorption and a different serologic profile, not a positive lactose breath test.
explanation_incorrect.B: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth can cause diarrhea and B12 malabsorption but does not produce the specific post-lactose hydrogen rise with low stool pH seen here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; D-xylose absorption remains normal and the lactose breath test would not be the diagnostic test.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bile acid diarrhea follows ileal disease or resection and causes watery stools, but it is not triggered specifically by lactose and does not lower stool pH through carbohydrate fermentation.

educationalObjective: Lactose intolerance causes osmotic diarrhea with low stool pH and a positive lactose hydrogen breath test with otherwise normal villi.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, Whipple
vignette: A 52-year-old man with a 6-year history of alcohol use disorder presents with bulky, foul-smelling stools and a 12-kg weight loss. He has no abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies show a normal D-xylose absorption test, decreased fecal elastase, and low levels of vitamins A and D.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's malabsorption?

options.text: Loss of distal ileal mucosa preventing bile salt reabsorption and fat emulsion
Immune-mediated villous blunting triggered by dietary gliadin in wheat
Bacterial fermentation of unabsorbed disaccharides in the colonic lumen
Defective enterocyte transporter for neutral amino acids in the proximal jejunum
Loss of pancreatic exocrine secretion with inability to digest fat and fat-soluble vitamins

explanation_correct: Chronic pancreatitis destroys exocrine tissue, causing pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K as well as vitamin B12. D-xylose is absorbed passively by the proximal small intestinal mucosa and remains normal, distinguishing pancreatic insufficiency from mucosal disease. Fecal elastase is reduced because it reflects acinar cell output.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ileal disease interrupts bile salt reabsorption and can cause bile acid diarrhea and oxalate stones, but it would not reduce fecal elastase or cause the described normal D-xylose pattern with low pancreatic enzymes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Celiac disease causes villous atrophy and would produce an abnormal D-xylose test plus positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, not a low fecal elastase.
explanation_incorrect.C: Carbohydrate malabsorption produces osmotic diarrhea rather than steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; the appropriate test would be a hydrogen breath test.
explanation_incorrect.D: A neutral amino acid transporter defect (Hartnup disease) affects tryptophan absorption and causes pellagra-like symptoms, not steatorrhea with low fecal elastase.

educationalObjective: Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea with normal D-xylose absorption and reduced fecal elastase.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, Whipple
vignette: A 41-year-old physician returns from 18 months of volunteer work in Southeast Asia with progressive diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. Laboratory evaluation shows megaloblastic anemia. Small bowel biopsy shows villous blunting similar to celiac disease, but a gluten-free diet produces no improvement. Symptoms resolve after a course of antibiotics.
question: Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?

options.text: Whipple disease, because it responds dramatically to antibiotic therapy
Celiac disease, because the histology and megaloblastic anemia are identical
Tropical sprue, because it affects the small bowel and responds to antibiotics
Pancreatic insufficiency, because it produces megaloblastic anemia from enzyme loss
Lactose intolerance, because it is common in residents of tropical regions

explanation_correct: Tropical sprue shows findings similar to celiac sprue, including small bowel villous blunting and malabsorption affecting the duodenum and jejunum, possibly the ileum with time. It occurs in residents of or recent visitors to the tropics and responds to antibiotics. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, with B12 deficiency developing later. Its cause is unknown.

explanation_incorrect.A: Whipple disease is a Tropheryma whipplei infection with PAS-positive foamy macrophages and cardiac, arthralgic, and neurologic features; diarrhea occurs late, and it is not the classic antibiotic-responsive syndrome in a traveler with folate deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.B: Celiac disease would be expected to improve on a gluten-free diet and is associated with HLA-DQ2/DQ8 and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, none of which is described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Chronic pancreatitis causes malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins with normal D-xylose, not megaloblastic anemia from folate loss or an antibiotic response.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lactose intolerance causes osmotic diarrhea with a positive breath test and normal villi; it would not cause megaloblastic anemia or villous blunting.

educationalObjective: Tropical sprue mimics celiac disease in the tropics and is distinguished by its response to antibiotics.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, Whipple
vignette: A 68-year-old man presents with several months of weight loss, arthralgias, and intermittent diarrhea. He also has cognitive slowing. Small bowel biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria. imaging reveals cardiac involvement.
question: Which infectious agent is most likely responsible?

options.text: Giardia lamblia, because it causes giardiasis with foul-smelling fatty diarrhea
Mycobacterium avium complex, because it infects macrophages in immunocompromised hosts
Clostridioides difficile, because it causes antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis
Tropheryma whipplei, because it causes Whipple disease with PAS-positive macrophages
Vibrio parahaemolyticus, because it causes watery diarrhea after seafood ingestion

explanation_correct: Whipple disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, an intracellular gram-positive bacillus. PAS-positive foamy macrophages fill the intestinal lamina propria. The classic mnemonic 'PASs the foamy Whipped cream in a CAN' refers to Cardiac symptoms, Arthralgias, and Neurologic symptoms; diarrhea and steatorrhea typically occur later in the disease course. It most commonly affects older males.

explanation_incorrect.A: Giardia produces fatty diarrhea without PAS-positive lamina propria macrophages or the cardiac, joint, and neurologic features described here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mycobacterium avium complex causes disseminated disease in severely immunocompromised patients and would show acid-fast organisms, not the characteristic PAS-positive foamy macrophages of Whipple disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: C difficile infection causes colonic pseudomembranes and watery diarrhea, usually after antibiotic exposure, and does not produce small bowel PAS-positive macrophages or arthralgias.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vibrio parahaemolyticus causes self-limited watery diarrhea after raw seafood ingestion, not a chronic multisystem syndrome with PAS-positive macrophages.

educationalObjective: Whipple disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei and shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages with cardiac, arthralgic, and neurologic features.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, Whipple
vignette: A 63-year-old man with chronic diarrhea and weight loss undergoes upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy. Histology shows accumulation of PAS-positive, diastase-resistant macrophages within the lamina propria. He reports a history of knee and wrist pain for two years and recently noted mild forgetfulness.
question: Which clinical feature typically appears LATE in the course of this disease?

options.text: Painful peripheral arthralgias
Cognitive change and neurologic symptoms
Cardiac murmurs from valvular involvement
Megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency
Diarrhea and steatorrhea

explanation_correct: In Whipple disease, the CAN features (Cardiac symptoms, Arthralgias, Neurologic symptoms) often precede the intestinal manifestations; diarrhea and steatorrhea occur later in the disease course. PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the intestinal lamina propria are the histologic hallmark.

explanation_incorrect.A: Arthralgias are among the early systemic 'CAN' manifestations and commonly precede the diagnosis of Whipple disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neurologic involvement, including cognitive change, is part of the classic CAN triad and can occur early or be the presenting feature.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cardiac symptoms are one of the CAN features and tend to appear as part of the early systemic phase rather than late intestinal disease.
explanation_incorrect.D: Folate deficiency with megaloblastic anemia is characteristic of tropical sprue, not a typical feature of Whipple disease.

educationalObjective: In Whipple disease, cardiac, joint, and neurologic symptoms typically precede the later diarrhea and steatorrhea.

subject: Gastrointestinal
subtopic: Lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, tropical sprue, Whipple
vignette: Two patients with chronic diarrhea undergo a D-xylose absorption test. The first has mucosal disease of the proximal small intestine; the second has chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency.
question: How are the D-xylose results expected to differ?

options.text: D-xylose absorption is reduced in the patient with mucosal disease but normal in the patient with pancreatic insufficiency
D-xylose absorption is reduced in both patients because both have malabsorption of nutrients
D-xylose absorption is normal in the patient with mucosal disease but reduced in pancreatic insufficiency
D-xylose absorption is elevated in both patients because of rapid intestinal transit
D-xylose cannot be used to distinguish these conditions because it requires pancreatic enzymes for absorption

explanation_correct: D-xylose is a simple sugar absorbed passively in the proximal small intestine without requiring pancreatic enzymes or bile salts. Blood and urine levels decrease with mucosal damage (for example, celiac disease), but remain normal in pancreatic insufficiency. This makes the test useful for distinguishing mucosal from pancreatic causes of malabsorption.

explanation_incorrect.B: D-xylose does not depend on pancreatic digestion, so patients with exocrine insufficiency absorb it normally despite steatorrhea.
explanation_incorrect.C: The pattern is reversed: mucosal disease reduces D-xylose absorption, whereas pancreatic insufficiency does not.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rapid transit generally reduces, not increases, measured D-xylose absorption, and elevated levels are not expected in either condition.
explanation_incorrect.E: D-xylose requires neither pancreatic enzymes nor micelles for uptake, which is precisely why it distinguishes mucosal from pancreatic disease.

educationalObjective: D-xylose absorption is abnormal with mucosal disease but normal in pancreatic insufficiency.
